quests.instruction: Say “come in” at normal speed, the way you would at a door. Which description matches how it sounds?
options: “Come” and “in” stay apart, with a short pause between them, like “come … in”
The /m/ at the end of “come” slides onto “in”, so it sounds like “cuh-min”
quests.correctAnswer: The /m/ at the end of “come” slides onto “in”, so it sounds like “cuh-min”
quests.hint: Imagine you are opening the door for a friend. Say it quickly and notice where the second word seems to begin.
quests.explanation: When a word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel, the consonant is usually heard at the start of the next syllable. In “come in”, the /m/ is pulled onto “in”, so you hear “cuh-min”. Noticing this helps you find word boundaries when people speak quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant sound is commonly pronounced as the beginning of the next syllable when the following word starts with a vowel, so the two words flow as one unit.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits what happens to the /v/ in “leave a message” when it is said naturally.
options: The /v/ is still there, but it is heard at the start of “a”: “lee-va message”
The /v/ is dropped so the two vowels can meet: “lee-a message”
quests.correctAnswer: The /v/ is still there, but it is heard at the start of “a”: “lee-va message”
quests.hint: Count the sounds you hear between “lee” and “message”, then decide whether one has been removed or simply placed somewhere new.
quests.explanation: Nothing is deleted here. The /v/ that finishes “leave” simply moves across and begins the next syllable, so you hear “lee-va”. This is why fast speech seems to run words together, even though every sound is still present.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking keeps the consonant sound but changes which syllable it belongs to: the final consonant of one word becomes the onset of the next vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Use what you noticed: which version matches natural speech for “look at this”?
options: “loo-kat this”, with the /k/ joined to “at”
“look, at, this”, with a clear break before “at”
quests.correctAnswer: “loo-kat this”, with the /k/ joined to “at”
quests.hint: Keep the same idea as before: a word that ends in a consonant meets a word that starts with a vowel. Which boundary in this phrase fits that description?
quests.explanation: “Look” ends in /k/ and “at” begins with a vowel, so the /k/ is heard at the start of “at”. The result is “loo-kat this”. There is no such link before “this”, because it begins with a consonant. Spotting the first chunk makes fast requests easier to follow.
quests.phoneticRule: The link happens only where a consonant sound meets a following vowel sound; a consonant followed by another consonant does not link in this way.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural spoken form of “drop off” in a sentence like “Could you drop off the keys?”
options: “drop … off”: the /p/ stays closed before a short pause
“dro-poff”: the /p/ joins the second word
quests.correctAnswer: “dro-poff”: the /p/ joins the second word
quests.hint: Say it three times, faster each time. On the last try, notice whether your mouth closes for the /p/ before a pause or just as “off” starts.
quests.explanation: The /p/ at the end of “drop” is followed by a vowel, so it links forward and “off” begins with the /p/: “dro-poff”. It also explains why fast speech can sound as if it contains an unfamiliar word like “poff”.
quests.phoneticRule: When a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the syllable boundary usually shifts so the consonant becomes the onset of the following word's first syllable.

quests.instruction: Which sound from “clean” is heard at the start of the second syllable in “clean up”?
options: The /n/, the last sound of “clean”
The /l/, from inside “clean”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/, the last sound of “clean”
quests.hint: Say “clean up” slowly, then speed up. Notice which sound your tongue is still making as “up” begins.
quests.explanation: Only the final sound of a word travels to the next word. In “clean up” that is /n/, so the syllables sound like “clee-nup”. Sounds inside the word, such as /l/, stay where they are.
quests.phoneticRule: Only the word-final consonant is re-attached to the next syllable; consonants earlier in the word keep their position.

quests.instruction: Apply the same idea to “hold on”. Which version sounds like fluent speech?
options: “hol-on”, with the /d/ left out because “on” begins with a vowel
“hol-don”, with the /d/ starting the second syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “hol-don”, with the /d/ starting the second syllable
quests.hint: Think of a phone call: “Hold on, I’ll check.” The /d/ ends the first word. Does it get lost, or does it hop across?
quests.explanation: Linking keeps the /d/ but places it at the start of the next syllable, giving “hol-don”. Learners sometimes drop the /d/ because a vowel follows, but the consonant is still part of the sound stream. Hearing it helps you recognise the phrase even when it comes quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: The consonant at the end of a word usually stays in the sound stream when a vowel follows; it is linked rather than dropped.

quests.instruction: Look at “turn it on”. Which words are connected when it is said naturally?
options: Only “turn it” joins; “on” stays apart because it comes last
“Turn” joins “it”, and “it” joins “on”, so the phrase moves as one chain
quests.correctAnswer: “Turn” joins “it”, and “it” joins “on”, so the phrase moves as one chain
quests.hint: Read the phrase aloud and mark each place where one word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, then count your marks.
quests.explanation: There are two boundaries and both fit the pattern: /n/ + vowel and /t/ + vowel. So you hear “tur-ni-ton”, one connected chain. Position in the phrase makes no difference to whether a link can happen.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking can repeat across a short chunk: each consonant-final word can hand its last sound to the vowel-initial word that follows.

quests.instruction: Why does “put it away” sound like “pu-ti-ta-way” in fast speech? Choose the best explanation.
options: Each word-final consonant is followed by a vowel, so the consonants shift onto the next syllables and the words chain together
The word “it” is left out in fast speech, so “put” and “away” are joined directly
quests.correctAnswer: Each word-final consonant is followed by a vowel, so the consonants shift onto the next syllables and the words chain together
quests.hint: Try leaving “it” out and compare “put away” with “put it away”. Which one matches the number of beats you hear in the fast version?
quests.explanation: Both /t/ sounds are still there. The first /t/ (from “put”) moves onto “it”, and the second /t/ (from “it”) moves onto “away”, giving four smooth beats. The small word is not deleted; it is tucked between its neighbours.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words such as “it” are usually kept when linking; they are built into the chain by receiving one consonant and passing on another.

quests.instruction: Choose the natural spoken chunking for “pass it on”.
options: “pass … it … on”: each word ends clearly, with a stop after every /s/ and /t/
“pa-si-ton”: /s/ moves to “it” and /t/ moves to “on”
quests.correctAnswer: “pa-si-ton”: /s/ moves to “it” and /t/ moves to “on”
quests.hint: Notice how many hisses you hear. If “pass” and “it” are joined, the /s/ should sound as if it belongs to the next word.
quests.explanation: The /s/ at the end of “pass” links to the vowel in “it”, and the /t/ links to “on”. Because /s/ is a long, continuous sound, the join is easy to hear: “pa-si-ton”. Expecting this makes phrases like “pass it on” easier to catch in group conversations.
quests.phoneticRule: Continuous consonants such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /n/ link very audibly, so they are good sounds to listen for when you search for word boundaries.

quests.instruction: Predict where the syllable break falls when you say “an apple” fluently.
options: “a-napple”: the /n/ starts the second syllable
“an-apple”: the /n/ stays with the first word
quests.correctAnswer: “a-napple”: the /n/ starts the second syllable
quests.hint: Clap once for each beat as you say it quickly. Does the /n/ sound like the end of a beat or the start of the next one?
quests.explanation: In natural speech, syllables are shaped by sounds, not by the spaces in writing. The /n/ from “an” is heard with “apple”, so the phrase sounds like “a-napple”. This is why a listener can briefly mistake the sound for a word that begins with “n”.
quests.phoneticRule: Spoken syllable boundaries follow the sound sequence rather than the spelling, so a final consonant can be heard as the start of the next word's first syllable.

quests.instruction: Why does “some of us” seem to have different syllable breaks from the written words?
options: Syllables are formed by the sounds you hear, so the /m/ and /v/ are heard at the start of the next syllables
Fast speech adds an extra syllable between the words to keep them apart
quests.correctAnswer: Syllables are formed by the sounds you hear, so the /m/ and /v/ are heard at the start of the next syllables
quests.hint: Write the phrase as you hear it in three quick beats and look at which consonants start them, then compare with the spelling of the words.
quests.explanation: “Some of us” is written as three words, but it is heard as “so-mo-vus”. The /m/ from “some” joins “of”, and the /v/ from “of” joins “us”. The number of syllables stays the same; only their edges move.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking shifts the edges of syllables without changing how many syllables a phrase contains.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea: which chunking matches the natural way to say “made a plan”?
options: “made-a-plan”: each word keeps its own final consonant, with a slight break after it
“may-da-plan”: the /d/ is heard at the start of “a”
quests.correctAnswer: “may-da-plan”: the /d/ is heard at the start of “a”
quests.hint: Look at the sound that ends “made”. What follows it, and what would your tongue naturally do next?
quests.explanation: The /d/ at the end of “made” meets the weak vowel of “a”, so it links: “may-da”. The phrase then continues into “plan”. Predicting the break correctly helps you hear three separate words instead of one unknown chunk.
quests.phoneticRule: Predicting a link starts with identifying the word-final consonant and checking whether the next word begins with a vowel sound.

quests.instruction: Someone thanks you for lending them a pen. Choose the reply that shows the natural chunking of “not at all”.
options: “no-ta-tall”: the /t/ of “not” joins “at”, and the /t/ of “at” joins “all”
“not / at / all”: three separate words, each with a clear break
quests.correctAnswer: “no-ta-tall”: the /t/ of “not” joins “at”, and the /t/ of “at” joins “all”
quests.hint: Imagine saying it warmly and quickly, with no effort to separate the words, and notice where the two /t/ sounds seem to belong.
quests.explanation: Both /t/ sounds sit before vowels, so each one is heard with the next syllable: “no-ta-tall”. The spelling shows three words, but the speech comes out as a smooth three-beat chain. Hearing it this way helps when someone answers quickly with everyday politeness.
quests.phoneticRule: Spelling hides where syllables start and end in speech; listening for the consonant + vowel boundary reveals the real chunking.

quests.instruction: The spelling shows two clear words, but the sound seems to differ. What explains the difference for “sign in”?
options: The word “in” becomes so weak that it merges into “sign” and stops being a separate word
The /n/ at the end of “sign” is heard at the start of “in”: “sai-nin”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ at the end of “sign” is heard at the start of “in”: “sai-nin”
quests.hint: Ignore the letters and write what you hear: the second syllable begins with a consonant. Which word does it come from?
quests.explanation: “Sign” has a silent “g”, but the pronunciation ends with /n/. That /n/ links to “in”, giving “sai-nin”. The second word is still there; it just seems to start a little earlier than the spelling suggests.
quests.phoneticRule: Pronunciation, not spelling, determines the word-final sound that links; silent letters play no part.

quests.instruction: Choose the fluent version of “half an hour”.
options: “half / an / hour”: each word stays separate, with a small stop before the vowel
“ha-fa-nour”: /f/ joins “an” and /n/ joins “hour”
quests.correctAnswer: “ha-fa-nour”: /f/ joins “an” and /n/ joins “hour”
quests.hint: Remember that “hour” begins with a vowel sound, not an “h”. Use that to decide what can attach to it.
quests.explanation: The /f/ of “half” links to “an”, and the /n/ of “an” links to “hour”, because “hour” starts with a vowel sound (the “h” is silent). The phrase becomes “ha-fa-nour”. It is a very common time expression, so it is worth recognising quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: The link depends on the first sound of the next word, not its first letter; words spelled with “h” can begin with a vowel sound.

quests.instruction: You hear a friend say “What is it?” quickly. Which form best matches the first two words?
options: “wo-tiz”, with the /t/ heard at the start of the second syllable
“wot-iz”, with the /t/ closing the first syllable and a break before “is”
quests.correctAnswer: “wo-tiz”, with the /t/ heard at the start of the second syllable
quests.hint: Notice where the /t/ falls if you say the two words with no pause. Does it end the first beat or open the second?
quests.explanation: Because “is” begins with a vowel, the /t/ from “what” often moves across, giving “wo-tiz”. Question openers like this are very common, so recognising the shift makes many questions easier to understand.
quests.phoneticRule: In question openers such as a wh-word plus a verb, a final consonant commonly links to the following vowel, shifting the syllable boundary.

quests.instruction: In “when is”, which final sound is heard at the start of the second syllable?
options: The /z/ of “is”, moving backwards onto the first word
The /n/ at the end of “when”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ at the end of “when”
quests.hint: Say it quickly and listen for the consonant that begins the second beat, then decide which word it originally belonged to.
quests.explanation: The /n/ that ends “when” links forward to the vowel in “is”, giving “we-niz”. The /z/ stays at the end of “is”, where it started. Sounds link forward in this pattern, not backward.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking moves a word-final consonant forward onto the next syllable; sounds do not shift backward onto the previous word.

quests.instruction: Use the pattern to choose the most natural spoken version of “what about”.
options: “wo-ta-bout”, with the /t/ joined to the weak vowel
“wot … a-bout”, with a pause after the /t/
quests.correctAnswer: “wo-ta-bout”, with the /t/ joined to the weak vowel
quests.hint: The second word starts with a very short vowel. Which sound just before it will attach to that vowel?
quests.explanation: The /t/ at the end of “what” attaches to the short first vowel of “about”, so it sounds like “wo-ta-bout”. It is a useful chunk in suggestions such as “What about Friday?”, where the link keeps the question smooth.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak, unstressed vowel at the start of a word, such as the /ə/ in “about”, readily receives a linked consonant.

quests.instruction: Listen for the boundary in “this is”. What best describes what you would hear?
options: A clear /s/ closing “this”, then a short break before “is”
The /s/ starts the second syllable: “thi-siz”
quests.correctAnswer: The /s/ starts the second syllable: “thi-siz”
quests.hint: Say it as if you are introducing a photo: “This is my sister.” Notice where the hissing sound sits in the two beats.
quests.explanation: “This” ends in /s/, and “is” begins with a vowel, so the /s/ links forward: “thi-siz”. Because /s/ is a long sound, the link is easy to hear once you know to listen for it.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /s/ and /z/ link to a following vowel just like stops and nasals, and the extra length of these sounds makes the join noticeable.

quests.instruction: Why does “yes it is” sound like a chain of small chunks instead of three words?
options: The /s/ and /t/ blend into a single new sound in the middle of the phrase
Both “yes” and “it” end in consonants that link to the vowel after them: “ye-si-tiz”
quests.correctAnswer: Both “yes” and “it” end in consonants that link to the vowel after them: “ye-si-tiz”
quests.hint: Count the beats you hear in the quick, agreeing reply. Then compare that number with the number of words on the page.
quests.explanation: “Yes” ends in /s/ and “it” ends in /t/, and each is followed by a vowel. So the /s/ links to “it” and the /t/ links to “is”, giving “ye-si-tiz”. Nothing blends into a new sound; each consonant just starts the next syllable.
quests.phoneticRule: Consecutive links create a chain: every consonant-final word followed by a vowel-initial word contributes its last sound to the next syllable.

quests.instruction: At the doctor’s, you hear “Does it hurt?” Which start matches natural speech?
options: “du-zit hurt”, with the /z/ joined to “it”
“duz … it hurt”, with the /z/ ending the first word and a stop before “it”
quests.correctAnswer: “du-zit hurt”, with the /z/ joined to “it”
quests.hint: Think about how a busy nurse would ask this quickly. The first word ends in a buzzing sound; where does that buzz land?
quests.explanation: “Does” ends with /z/, and “it” starts with a vowel, so you hear “du-zit”. The last word, “hurt”, has no link before it because it begins with a consonant. This pattern appears in many everyday questions such as “is it” and “does it”.
quests.phoneticRule: In yes/no questions, auxiliary verbs ending in /z/ typically link into the pronoun “it”, creating a compact first chunk.

quests.instruction: Predict which two consonants change position in “check it out”.
options: The /k/ of “check” and the /t/ of “it”
The /tʃ/ at the start of “check” and the /t/ at the end of “out”
quests.correctAnswer: The /k/ of “check” and the /t/ of “it”
quests.hint: Only sounds that end a word and meet a vowel can move. Look for those two spots in the phrase.
quests.explanation: The /k/ ending “check” meets the vowel in “it”, and the /t/ ending “it” meets the vowel in “out”, so both move: “che-ki-tout”. The first sound of the phrase and the last one stay where they are, because they have no link partner here.
quests.phoneticRule: A consonant can link only when it closes a word that is followed by a vowel-initial word, so the first and last sounds of a phrase have no link partner within it.

quests.instruction: Why does the small word “it” seem to disappear in “leave it alone”?
options: It is deleted in fast speech because the meaning is already clear from “leave” and “alone”
It is still there, but the /v/ from “leave” attaches in front of it and its own /t/ moves on to “alone”
quests.correctAnswer: It is still there, but the /v/ from “leave” attaches in front of it and its own /t/ moves on to “alone”
quests.hint: Slow it down to four beats and see whether “it” has a vowel of its own. Then speed up again.
quests.explanation: “It” is short and unstressed, so it is easy to miss. But it keeps its vowel and its /t/: the /v/ from “leave” attaches in front of it, and its own /t/ attaches to “alone”. Listeners who expect “it” can find it inside the chain.
quests.phoneticRule: Short function words can look absent in fast speech, but in linked speech they are still present, surrounded by the consonants that connect them to their neighbours.

quests.instruction: Choose the version of “read it aloud” that shows the links.
options: “ree-di-ta-loud”, with /d/ and /t/ each starting the next syllable
“read / it / a-loud”, each with a small break before the vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “ree-di-ta-loud”, with /d/ and /t/ each starting the next syllable
quests.hint: There are two word-final consonants followed by vowels here. Find both and think where each one lands.
quests.explanation: The /d/ that ends “read” links to “it”, and the /t/ that ends “it” links to “aloud”. The result is four smooth beats, “ree-di-ta-loud”. Try saying it once with each word separated and once with links; the connected version is closer to what you hear in real conversation.
quests.phoneticRule: Two links in a row follow the same logic as one: identify each word-final consonant and the vowel that follows it.

quests.instruction: One speaker says “look … after … Sam” with pauses. Another says it fluently. What is the main difference?
options: The fluent speaker puts a small pause before “after” so its vowel stands out clearly
The fluent speaker lets the /k/ of “look” slide onto “after”: “loo-kafter Sam”
quests.correctAnswer: The fluent speaker lets the /k/ of “look” slide onto “after”: “loo-kafter Sam”
quests.hint: Imagine asking a colleague quickly, with no time to spare. Would you stop before a vowel-initial word, or move straight through?
quests.explanation: Fluent speakers usually link instead of stopping. The /k/ moves to “after”, so you hear “loo-kafter”. Slow, word-by-word speech is fine for emphasis, but it is not the normal rhythm of conversation, and expecting it makes fast speech harder to follow.
quests.phoneticRule: In everyday speech, vowel-initial words are commonly linked to the preceding word rather than separated by a pause, though careful or emphatic speech may separate them.

quests.instruction: Which statement about “take a seat” is the most accurate?
options: Linked as “tay-ka seat”, it matches the rhythm listeners expect; separating every word can sound stiff
Separating every word is the clearest choice, because each consonant is then fully heard
quests.correctAnswer: Linked as “tay-ka seat”, it matches the rhythm listeners expect; separating every word can sound stiff
quests.hint: Think of a friendly welcome in an office and decide whether the speaker would say each word like a list or as one flowing invitation.
quests.explanation: The /k/ at the end of “take” joins the weak “a”, giving “tay-ka seat”. This is the flow listeners expect in conversation. Word-by-word delivery is easy to follow at a slow pace, but it can sound stiff and it does not train your ear for real speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Natural rhythm is built from linked chunks; word-by-word delivery is a useful slow-speech tool but not the default pattern of conversation.

quests.instruction: Say “old enough” like a fluent speaker. Which chunking shows the link?
options: “ol-di-nuff”, with the /d/ moving to the start of “enough”
“old … enough”, with a small stop before the first vowel of “enough”
quests.correctAnswer: “ol-di-nuff”, with the /d/ moving to the start of “enough”
quests.hint: The first word ends in a consonant cluster, and the second begins with a short vowel. Think about which part of the cluster sits right next to that vowel.
quests.explanation: In “old”, the final /d/ links to the vowel at the start of “enough”, giving “ol-di-nuff”. The /l/ stays where it is. The pattern also works after consonant clusters, so it is not limited to single final consonants.
quests.phoneticRule: When a word ends in a consonant cluster, generally only the final consonant of the cluster links to a following vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Identify what happens at the boundary between “sit” and “up”.
options: A silent break separates the words, and both keep their own sounds
The /t/ of “sit” moves onto “up”, so it sounds like “si-tup”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “sit” moves onto “up”, so it sounds like “si-tup”
quests.hint: A parent might say this quickly. Listen for what the /t/ seems to attach to once “up” arrives.
quests.explanation: The word “sit” ends in /t/, and “up” starts with a vowel, so the /t/ links forward: “si-tup”. This is the same pattern you have met in all the earlier levels: consonant, then vowel, then a joined syllable.
quests.phoneticRule: Recognising a linking environment requires two checks: the first word ends in a consonant sound, and the second begins with a vowel sound.

quests.instruction: Compare “good idea” with “good plan”. Why does only one of them sound linked?
options: “Idea” starts with a vowel, so the /d/ of “good” can join it; “plan” starts with a consonant, so there is nothing to attach to
“Plan” is a shorter word, and short words are too small to link with the word before
quests.correctAnswer: “Idea” starts with a vowel, so the /d/ of “good” can join it; “plan” starts with a consonant, so there is nothing to attach to
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “idea” with the first sound of “plan”. What kind of sound follows the /d/ in each?
quests.explanation: Linking needs a vowel after the consonant. “Idea” starts with one, giving “goo-didea”. “Plan” starts with /p/, so “good plan” has no consonant-to-vowel link; any other changes there are a separate topic. Word length is not what matters.
quests.phoneticRule: A vowel sound at the start of the next word is the condition for consonant-to-vowel linking; word length and word class are not the deciding factor.

quests.instruction: You hear someone comment on a missed chance: “Such a shame.” Which chunking fits fluent speech?
options: “such / a / shame”, with the /tʃ/ closing the first word and a stop after it
“su-cha shame”, with the /tʃ/ starting the second syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “su-cha shame”, with the /tʃ/ starting the second syllable
quests.hint: The first word ends with a “ch” sound. Listen for whether that sound closes the word or starts the next syllable.
quests.explanation: The /tʃ/ (the “ch” sound) that ends “such” links to “a”, giving “su-cha shame”. Consonants of many kinds link this way, including affricates, so the pattern is not limited to simple stops.
quests.phoneticRule: Every consonant sound, including affricates like /tʃ/, can link to a following vowel; the type of consonant does not prevent the link.
